title: What Education Can Learn From Zig Engelmann
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues that Siegfried "Zig" Engelmann's lasting contribution to education is not the Direct Instruction curriculum itself but the obsessive process he used to build it: relentless content analysis paired with empirical testing lesson by lesson. Kane illustrates Engelmann's method of teaching "categorical concepts" through carefully sequenced examples and non-examples, using his own classroom problem of students confusing multiplication and subtraction notation as a worked example. He describes how Engelmann's programs placed students by assessed skill rather than age or grade, allowing multiple cohorts to move through the same lesson at different times so the curriculum could be continuously tested and revised based on whether students actually learned. That empiricism was validated at scale by Project Follow Through, in which Direct Instruction outperformed rival approaches not just on basic skills but, counterintuitively, on problem-solving and self-esteem as well. Kane notes that despite this evidence, Direct Instruction never achieved wide adoption, which he attributes largely to Engelmann's disinterest in evangelizing rather than any failure of the method itself. He closes by pointing to two contemporary approaches inspired by Engelmann's spirit -- Judith Hochman's Writing Revolution and Kris Boulton's "atomisation" method -- as models of what it looks like to bring obsessive content analysis and empirical rigor back into teacher practice.
points: Engelmann's true legacy, per Kane, is his process -- obsessive analysis of content into "categorical concepts," taught through carefully sequenced examples and non-examples -- rather than the specific Direct Instruction scripts he produced.

Engelmann's programs placed students by an initial assessment rather than age or grade, which let multiple groups move through the same lesson at different times and let him test and revise the curriculum lesson by lesson based on whether students actually learned it.

In Project Follow Through, often called the largest educational experiment ever conducted, Direct Instruction outperformed rival curricula not only on basic skills but also, unexpectedly, on problem-solving and self-esteem.
Despite this evidence, Direct Instruction remains a minor player in U.S. schools, which Kane attributes to Engelmann's weak evangelism rather than a failure of the underlying method.

Kane points to Judith Hochman's Writing Revolution and Kris Boulton's "atomisation" approach as modern examples of Engelmann's spirit -- analyzing content deeply and testing ideas empirically in real classrooms -- applied to writing and math instruction today.
quotes: Siegfried (Zig) Engelmann was the lead author of the Direct Instruction curriculum programs. The first thing to understand about Engelmann is that he was absolutely obsessed with analyzing the content that we ask students to learn.

To Engelmann, there was no one ideal, content-agnostic way to teach. There was no default lesson plan, no structure that would work for every single piece of content. But he also didn't try to design each lesson from scratch.
After each lesson, he would ask a simple question: Did the students learn? If they didn't learn, something needed to change.

He called the end result "logically faultless communication." If students were correctly placed in the program and the content to be learned was analyzed correctly and the instruction delivered effectively and students engaged with the lesson, every student should learn.

Direct Instruction is unashamedly a "basic skills" model so it might be unsurprising that it did best with basic skills. What surprises many people is that Direct Instruction performed best with problem-solving skills and self-esteem as well.
Engelmann was an empiricist. He believed that the evidence for the empirical success of his programs should be enough to convince schools to adopt Direct Instruction. He wasn't very successful.
We need fewer abstract arguments about teaching in general, and more work deep in the weeds of content and the concrete details that ensure each student learns.
